practical.heading: Your dates: a holiday weekend
items: Fri 25 Dec (Christmas Day) and Sat 26 Dec (first weekday after Christmas) are both general and statutory holidays in 2026; Sun 27 Dec is a normal Sunday. Banks and government offices close 25–26 Dec.

Expect peak crowds all three days: locals off work plus a mainland-visitor surge. Book popular restaurants, harbour cruises and anything ticketed in advance, and expect long queues at the Peak Tram, Ngong Ping 360 and famous cha chaan teng.
Small family-run shops, craftsmen and some dai pai dong close for Christmas Day and/or Sundays. Check individual cards for notes.

Christmas Eve (the night before you arrive) is when MTR runs overnight; on 24 Dec 2025 eight lines ran all night and Central had road closures from 2pm. Expect a similar pattern in 2026, but it doesn't directly affect 25–27 Dec.

A Symphony of Lights, the nightly harbour light show, was suspended on 9 Sep 2026 pending a new format. Don't plan around 8pm on the promenade unless a replacement is announced. Skyline views at blue hour are still worth it.
Horse racing: Sha Tin holds a day meeting on Sat 26 Dec, confirmed on HKJC's fixture calendar (none on 25 or 27 Dec). Fixtures can change, so re-check close to the date.

practical.heading: Daylight & weather
items: Hong Kong Observatory times: sunrise 07:00, sunset 17:46 (25 Dec) / 17:47 (26–27 Dec). Golden hour is roughly 16:45–17:45 and blue hour roughly 17:45–18:15. Plan skyline and hilltop shots around them.

December averages ~15–21 °C, low humidity (~70%) and very little rain (~27 mm for the whole month). It's the clearest, most comfortable month for hiking and skyline photos. A cold surge can drop lows to around 10 °C, and regional haze sometimes softens distant views.
Bring a light jacket for evenings, harbour ferries and hilltops; indoor air-conditioning is still strong.

practical.heading: Getting around
items: Octopus card (or Octopus in Apple Wallet) works on MTR, trams, buses, minibuses, ferries, convenience stores and many shops. It's still the most universal option.

Contactless Visa/Mastercard/UnionPay credit cards can be tapped at designated MTR heavy-rail gates (adult fares). Airport Express, Light Rail and MTR buses may not accept them, so check MTR's site before relying on them.
Trams (one cheap flat fare, tap Octopus as you exit) and the Star Ferry are both transport and sightseeing. Green minibuses take Octopus. Many red minibuses are cash-only.
Holiday-weekend crowds hit Sai Kung buses, the Dragon's Back bus (No. 9), Tung Chung cable-car queues and outlying-island ferries hardest. Go early.

practical.heading: Money & etiquette
items: Cards and AlipayHK/WeChat Pay HK work in most restaurants and malls. Carry some HKD cash for street stalls, older cha chaan teng, wet markets, red minibuses and small temples.
Many sit-down restaurants add a 10% service charge. Tipping on top isn't expected; leaving small change at cha chaan teng is a courtesy, not a rule.
Expect to share tables (搭枱) at busy local spots. Order quickly, eat, and don't linger at peak hours.
At dim sum, rinsing your cups and bowls with the first pot of tea is common, and tapping two fingers on the table thanks whoever pours.

practical.heading: Day trips across the border
items: Macau: TurboJET or Cotai Water Jet ferries (about 1 h) or the HZMB shuttle bus from the airport area. Bring your passport. Holiday-weekend ferries sell out, so book ahead.

Shenzhen: as of Oct 2026, mainland China's 30-day visa-free entry covers citizens of roughly 45–50 countries through 31 Dec 2026. Confirm your own nationality's rules before going, and remember 25–27 Dec border crossings are very busy.

overview.heading: What Hong Kong is known for
overview.text: A vertical harbour city where Cantonese food culture runs from Michelin-starred dining rooms to plastic stools: dim sum and yum cha, siu mei roast meats, wonton noodles, cha chaan teng milk tea, and late-night dai pai dong. The city sits on three layers: colonial-era Central, dense post-war tong lau and public estates, and steep green country parks that cover about 40% of the land and start minutes from the skyline.

overview.heading: Neighbourhoods worth wandering
overview.text: Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun (dried-seafood streets, antiques, cafés), Tai Hang (village lanes under Causeway Bay), Sham Shui Po (fabric, leather, electronics and maker shops, plus the hip café wave), Yau Ma Tei and Mong Kok (themed market streets, the night market, surviving neon), To Kwa Wan's 13 Streets, Quarry Bay's estates, and slower island villages at Tai O, Cheung Chau and Peng Chau.

overview.heading: Shopping & design
overview.text: Malls are everywhere, so the distinctive layer is elsewhere: heritage pantry brands (Kowloon Soy, Kee Wah, Wing Wah, Garden), last-of-their-trade craftsmen (bamboo steamers, bird cages, cheongsam, neon), PMQ and Tai Kwun design shops, film-camera dealers, and Sham Shui Po's craft-supply streets. Small family shops are disappearing quickly, so treat every old-shop entry as worth confirming.

overview.heading: Your dates
overview.text: Fri 25 and Sat 26 Dec are both public holidays and Sun 27 Dec is a Sunday, so the whole trip is a holiday weekend: big crowds, festive lights, and some small shops, craftsmen and noodle shops closed on Christmas Day or Sundays. December is the driest, clearest month (about 15–21 °C), so it's peak hiking and skyline season. Sunset is about 17:46, with blue hour around 17:45–18:15. Winter dishes are in season: claypot rice, snake soup, hot pot, street-cart chestnuts and lap mei.

clusters.name: Central: Hollywood Road, SoHo & Tai Kwun
clusters.summary: The steep grid above Queen's Road holds the heritage-and-design core (Tai Kwun, PMQ, G.O.D.), the escalator, the Graham Street market, and the densest run of old-school eating: Kau Kee, Sing Heung Yuen, Luk Yu, Yat Lok, Tai Cheong egg tarts. The bars are along Wyndham and Peel Streets.

clusters.name: Central harbourfront
clusters.summary: Statue Square's WinterFest Christmas Town, IFC, the Four Seasons (Lung King Heen, Argo), the Maritime Museum and the Star Ferry piers.

clusters.name: Sheung Wan & Sai Ying Pun
clusters.summary: Dried-seafood and herbal streets, Man Mo Temple, Cat Street antiques, a bamboo-steamer maker and claypot rice, running west into Sai Ying Pun's cafés and the old cargo pier.

clusters.name: Kennedy Town
clusters.summary: End of the tram line: harbourfront promenade for sunsets, claypot rice and a late-night local diner.

clusters.name: Wan Chai
clusters.summary: Roast goose, congee, the Blue House heritage cluster, and Lee Tung Avenue's festive street.

clusters.name: North Point to Quarry Bay
clusters.summary: The eastern tram corridor: egg waffles in North Point, the Braemar Hill lookout above, and the Monster Building estates at Quarry Bay.

clusters.name: The Peak
clusters.summary: Peak Tram up, then the flat Lugard Road loop for the classic skyline at golden and blue hour.

clusters.name: Tsim Sha Tsui harbourfront
clusters.summary: The Star Ferry pier, the promenade and Avenue of Stars, the Ocean Terminal Deck, HKMoA, the Cultural Centre (Nutcracker), Harbour City and K11 MUSEA, plus Chiu Chow food and the Haiphong Road hawker bazaar.

clusters.name: West Kowloon Cultural District
clusters.summary: M+, the Palace Museum and Xiqu Centre on one waterfront park, with the sunset promenade, plus sky100 and OZONE in the ICC tower next door.

clusters.name: Jordan & Yau Ma Tei
clusters.summary: Cha chaan teng breakfasts, wonton noodles and sweet soup by day; Temple Street, late-night skewers, Mido's corner and the fruit market after dark.

clusters.name: Mong Kok & Prince Edward
clusters.summary: Themed market streets (Ladies', Sneakers, Goldfish, Flower Market, Bird Garden), film-camera shops, neon, Lui Seng Chun, Kam Wah's pineapple buns and a roastery.

clusters.name: Sham Shui Po
clusters.summary: Fabric, leather and electronics streets, Apliu flea market, Michelin cheap eats (Tim Ho Wan, Hop Yik Tai, Lau Sum Kee), Mei Ho House and new roasters and vintage shops.

clusters.name: Kowloon City & To Kwa Wan
clusters.summary: Old Kai Tak's flight-path district: Thai and Chiu Chow food, satay-beef hot pot, the 13 Streets grid and a dai pai dong.

clusters.name: Wong Tai Sin, Diamond Hill & Choi Hung
clusters.summary: Wong Tai Sin Temple and its fortune-tellers, Chi Lin Nunnery and Nan Lian Garden one stop on, and the Choi Hung and Ping Shek estates.

clusters.name: Sai Kung
clusters.summary: Seafood on the waterfront, kaito boats to Yim Tin Tsai, and the East Dam geo trail and Sai Wan beaches beyond.

clusters.name: Ngong Ping & Tai O (Lantau)
clusters.summary: The cable car to the Big Buddha and the Lantau Peak trailhead; a short bus ride down to Tai O's stilt houses, sampans and shrimp paste.

clusters.name: Tai Mei Tuk & Plover Cove
clusters.summary: Reservoir dam and cycling at Tai Mei Tuk, which is also the start of the Pat Sin Leng ridge.
